```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5,
                      warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

A DietView sunburst shows the diet at seven ranks at once, from kingdom at the
center to species at the edge. This article explains what a percentage in any
ring is a percentage of, and why prey that could not be identified to a given
rank stay in the figure instead of being dropped. It uses the Atlantic cod
records of the public ICES stomach data that ship with the package (ICES
Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R
package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see `?ices_diet`).

```{r setup}
library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)

cod  <- dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]
prep <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
tree <- dv_build_tree(prep$data, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
```

The cod data hold `r format(nrow(cod), big.mark = ",")` prey records from
`r length(unique(cod$stomach_id))` stomachs.

## One record, one place in every ring

`dv_build_tree()` gives every record one place at every rank: the taxon
it was identified to at that rank or, if identification stopped earlier, an
unidentified node (`NA` in the tables) below the last rank it reached. Three
cod prey records show the range:

```{r three-records}
ex <- match(c("Crangon crangon", "Brachyura", "Pisces"), prep$data$prey_name)
prep$data[ex, c("prey_name", prep$ranks)]
```

A brown shrimp (*Crangon crangon*) sits under Decapoda at order and under
*Crangon* at genus. A crab named only "Brachyura" sits under Decapoda at order
and in the unidentified node below Decapoda at family, genus and species. A
fish named only "Pisces" sits under Chordata at phylum and in the unidentified
node below Chordata from class outward.

So every ring holds the same records and the same weight:

```{r totals}
rings <- unique(tree$rank)
data.frame(
  rank      = rings,
  records   = sapply(rings, function(r) sum(tree$value_occ[tree$rank == r])),
  weight_g  = sapply(rings, function(r) round(sum(tree$value_w[tree$rank == r]), 1)),
  pct_total = sapply(rings, function(r) round(sum(tree$pct_occ[tree$rank == r]), 1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

Each percentage in the tree (`pct_occ` for records, `pct_w` for weight) is a
node's value divided by that common total, and each ring adds up to 100%. The
weight total is lower than it would be with every record weighed: the
`r sum(is.na(cod$prey_weight_g))` cod records without a weight count in the
records currency and add nothing to the weight one.

Because no record is lost between rings, a node's value is also the sum of its
children's values, which is what lets the rings nest:

```{r nesting}
kids <- tapply(tree$value_occ, tree$parent, sum)
parents <- tree[tree$id %in% names(kids), ]
all.equal(parents$value_occ, as.numeric(kids[parents$id]))
all.equal(parents$value_w, as.numeric(tapply(tree$value_w, tree$parent, sum)[parents$id]))
```

Both checks hold for the `r nrow(parents)` nodes that have children, in
records and in weight.

## What dropping the unidentified records would do

The usual alternative is to drop, at each rank, the records that were not
identified to that rank, and to compute shares among the rest. Each ring then
has its own total, and the rings stop agreeing with each other:

```{r dropped}
id_only <- function(r) tree[tree$rank == r & tree$label != "NA", ]
share_in <- function(r, pattern) {
  x <- id_only(r)
  100 * sum(x$value_occ[grepl(pattern, x$id, fixed = TRUE)]) / sum(x$value_occ)
}
mal <- c(class  = share_in("Class",  "|Malacostraca"),
         order  = share_in("Order",  "|Malacostraca|"),
         family = share_in("Family", "|Malacostraca|"),
         genus  = share_in("Genus",  "|Malacostraca|"))
round(mal, 1)
```

Malacostraca would be `r round(mal[["class"]], 1)`% of the identified records
at class, its orders together `r round(mal[["order"]], 1)`% of the identified
records at order, its families `r round(mal[["family"]], 1)`% at family and its
genera `r round(mal[["genus"]], 1)`% at genus. Nothing about the diet changed
between the rings; only the set of records did. Each ring drops a different
set of records (at family, the crabs named only "Brachyura" and the shrimps
named only "Caridea"; at genus, also the swimming crabs named only
Polybiidae), so the crustacean share swings with the
identification habits of the people who read the stomachs. With the
unidentified records kept, Malacostraca and everything below it hold the same
`r tree$value_occ[tree$label == "Malacostraca"]` records in every ring:
`r round(tree$pct_occ[tree$label == "Malacostraca"], 1)`% of the cod's prey
records.

## How much was not identified, and where

`dv_rank_table()` lists one ring. The unidentified records do not form one
`NA` row: there is one per parent, so you can tell what kind of prey stopped
being identified at that rank. At order:

```{r na}
ord <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Order")
na_rows <- tree[tree$rank == "Order" & tree$label == "NA",
                c("parent", "value_occ", "pct_occ")]
na_rows$pct_occ <- round(na_rows$pct_occ, 2)
na_rows[order(-na_rows$value_occ), ]
sum(ord$pct_occ[ord$label == "NA"])
```

```{r na-num, include = FALSE}
na_ord <- sum(ord$pct_occ[ord$label == "NA"])
top <- na_rows[order(-na_rows$value_occ), ][1:3, ]
```

Here `r round(na_ord, 1)`% of the records are unidentified at order. The
largest parts are the material placed nowhere (parent `NA|NA|NA`), the fish
not identified beyond Chordata ("Pisces" and the like), and the crustaceans
named only "Crustacea" (parent `Animalia|Arthropoda|NA`). Report the total next to any statement made at that rank: an
order-level description of this diet rests on the remaining
`r round(100 - na_ord, 1)`%. The per-parent rows say what the gap is made of,
which matters as much as its size: a gap made of fish and a gap made of worms
bias a description in different directions.

The share rises toward the edge of the sunburst:

```{r na-by-rank}
sapply(rings, function(r) round(sum(tree$pct_occ[tree$rank == r & tree$label == "NA"]), 1))
```

## An unidentified node with named children

Most `NA` nodes have only `NA` below them. A few do not, because WoRMS gives no
taxon at one rank to some groups. In the ICES lineage, several polychaete
families have no order, and Priapulida have no class:

```{r na-children}
kid_named <- tapply(tree$label != "NA", tree$parent, any)
na_with_kids <- tree[tree$label == "NA" & tree$id %in% names(kid_named)[kid_named], ]
na_with_kids[, c("id", "rank", "value_occ")]
tree[tree$parent %in% na_with_kids$id & tree$label != "NA", c("parent", "label", "value_occ")]
```

```{r na-children-num, include = FALSE}
n_poly <- na_with_kids$value_occ[na_with_kids$rank == "Order"]
```

Such a node mixes two things. The `r n_poly` cod records in the unidentified
order node under Polychaeta are `r n_poly - 1` polychaetes not identified
beyond class and one lugworm (Arenicolidae), a family to which WoRMS gives no
order: identified to family, it still appears unidentified at order. The
effect is one record here, but on another predator or survey it can be
large. Before you
report an unidentified share at that rank, check these rows; the article
"Adapting DietView to your own survey" comes back to it.

## The figures

Records first, then weight. In cod the two currencies rank prey very
differently, so look at both before choosing one to report.

```{r sunburst-occ}
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", title = "Atlantic cod",
            subtitle = "share of prey records")
```

```{r sunburst-w}
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "weight", title = "Atlantic cod",
            subtitle = "share of prey weight")
```

White wedges with gray edges are records not identified at that rank. Hovering
over a wedge shows its count and its share of the ring.

## Colors

`dv_palette()` gives each taxon name one color and unidentified nodes white.
Build it once from all the records and pass it to every figure you want to
compare, so the same taxon has the same color everywhere:

```{r palette}
pal <- dv_palette(tree$label)
length(pal)
head(pal)
```

The palette has 20 colors and reuses them when there are more taxa. The cod
tree alone has `r length(pal) - 1` taxon names, so every color stands for
about `r round((length(pal) - 1) / 20)` of them. Check the hover labels before
you read a color as a taxon.

`dv_palette_tree()` is the better choice at this size. It gives one hue to
each phylum (the second rank) and lighter tints of that hue to its
descendants, and keeps unidentified nodes white. Its colors are keyed by node,
so build it from the pooled tree and pass it to every panel in the same way:

```{r palette-tree}
pal_tree <- dv_palette_tree(tree)
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal_tree, title = "Atlantic cod",
            subtitle = "share of prey records, colors by phylum")
```
